Thursday in the cab
Thursday, 13 November, evening. Costel’s lorry is parked outside Señor Dan’s block of flats. The two of them are studying for next Saturday’s DELE B2 exam. Ana brings them one last practice test.
I don’t know what’s wrong with me, Ana. The more I study, the less I know. Yesterday I understood the subjunctive and today I don’t.
It’s normal. The closer the exam gets, the more nervous you get. But you’re making fewer and fewer mistakes.
I’ve made a table. Costel studies twice as much as I do, but I sleep twice as much as he does.
And you’re just as nervous as I am, even if you hide it behind your tables.
You’re both better prepared than you think. In the last practice test you got more points than you need.
And the listening comprehension? The recordings are incredibly fast.
Not so much for me any more. I’ve been listening to the weather forecast for three months. Now I understand it almost as well as in Romanian.
Then on Saturday, eat well, sleep eight hours and don’t study anything on Friday. That’s the most important thing of all.
Nothing? That’s harder than the exam.
Costel’s right. For us, not studying is as complicated as it gets.

The stress always moves to “-ÍS-”: ra-pi-DÍ-si-mo, ner-vio-SÍ-si-mo, ca-RÍ-si-mo. Adjectives in -co / -go change a letter: rico → riquísimo, largo → larguísimo.
Say “cuanto más” as one unit, stressing “más”: [kuan-to-MAS]. In the second clause, “más” or “menos” is stressed just as strongly.
The “b” between vowels is soft, almost like a “v” without the teeth: [el-DO-ble]. Don’t pronounce it like a hard English “b”.

Consejos para el día del examen
A sheet Ana gives all her students before the DELE. Notice the comparisons.
The more rested you arrive, the better you’ll perform. Sleeping well the night before is as important as having studied for months.
In the listening comprehension, don’t try to understand everything. The recordings are incredibly fast, but the questions are usually simpler than they seem.
In written expression, it’s better to write short, correct sentences than long sentences with mistakes. A clear text is worth twice as much as a complicated one.
In the oral test, the examiner isn’t looking for someone perfect, but for someone who communicates. The more natural you are, the more points you’ll get.

El examen

Since mid-October, Costel’s lorry had spent Thursday evenings parked outside Señor Dan’s block of flats, on a quiet street in Drumul Taberei. At first the neighbours complained, because it took up three parking spaces. But when they found out that inside were two men over fifty studying Spanish for an exam, the building’s administrator brought them down a flask of tea and told them they could park there for as long as they needed.

The two of them studied in completely different ways. Señor Dan organised everything in tables: irregular verbs in columns, connectors by colour, study hours calculated to the minute. Costel, on the other hand, studied the way he drove: from memory, by intuition and with the radio on. The tidier Señor Dan was, the messier Costel seemed. And yet in the practice tests they got almost the same mark, which made Señor Dan as nervous as can be.

Over time, each began to learn something from the other. Señor Dan explained long sentences to Costel by drawing them as bridges: the subject was one pillar, the main verb another pillar, and the subordinate clauses were the arches joining them. Costel, in return, taught him not to translate every word in his head, but to listen to the music of the sentence, the way you listen to an engine to know whether it’s running well. The more they practised like this, the less the differences between them showed. By the end of October, Señor Dan was listening to the radio in his car, and Costel had made his first table.

Ana couldn’t examine them, because she worked at the Instituto Cervantes and it would have been a conflict of interest. But on Thursdays she brought them practice tests and a stopwatch. She had also given them a sheet of tips for exam day, which Señor Dan had laminated and stuck on the dashboard. Costel knew it by heart. He recited it aloud at traffic lights, to the despair of drivers who saw him talking to himself in his cab.

A week before the exam, Costel had a crisis. He called Ana at eleven at night from a car park near Arad and told her he wasn’t going to sit it. That the more he studied, the less he knew. That he had completely forgotten the subjunctive. That at his age you couldn’t learn anything new. Ana listened to him for twenty minutes without interrupting. Then she asked him how to say “I’ve forgotten the subjunctive” in Spanish. Costel answered without thinking: “Es que no creo que lo recuerde.” Ana laughed. It took him a moment to understand why.

The next day Zoltán called him from a petrol station in Hungary. He had heard about the crisis, because news among lorry drivers travels faster than lorries. Zoltán still knew only thirty words of Spanish, but he had prepared a sentence specially for the occasion, with the help of a translation app: “Costel, you stronger than lorry. Exam smaller than Hungary.” Costel told him it made no sense at all. Zoltán said it didn’t matter, what mattered was that he had understood it. And it was true.

In Madrid, meanwhile, November had arrived with cold and rain. Andrei had taken his father’s advice and bought a coat. Begoña was sending him on harder and harder jobs: a pensioners’ demonstration, a football match in the rain, a fire in a warehouse in Vallecas. He came home soaked and exhausted, but happier and happier. Lucas said Andrei now took photos almost as well as he did, and that this worried him enormously.

One Sunday, Andrei went to the Cuesta de Moyano to see Faustino. The five-hundred-peseta note was already framed and hanging in the stall, next to a photo of Andrés that Faustino had found in another box. Customers asked about it, and Faustino told the story with so many new details each time that Lucas, who went with him that day, calculated that within a year the Neruda debt would be as long as Don Quixote. Andrei took a photo of the stall to send to Ecaterina. Faustino posed in his red beret, very seriously, like a minister.

Ecaterina, for her part, had already written two thirds of the book. The further she got, the more slowly she wrote, because she was approaching the hardest chapters: the autumn of 1987, the phone call from Bucharest, the suitcase packed in one night, the letter she didn’t send. She had told Inés Vidal she would have the manuscript finished before Christmas. Inés had replied that there was no hurry. Ecaterina had answered that there was for her, because at her age Christmas was a very serious deadline.

Mrs Florica prepared in her own way too. On Thursday she went to the neighbourhood church and lit two candles, one for each of them. Costel’s was twice as big as Señor Dan’s. When Ana asked her why, Mrs Florica explained, perfectly logically, that Costel studied twice as much and got twice as nervous, so he needed twice as much help. Señor Dan was not amused when he found out. But that same afternoon he went to the church on his own and lit another candle, a little bigger.

On the Friday before the exam, Ana banned them from studying. Señor Dan half obeyed: he didn’t open his books, but went over his tables in his head all through dinner, moving his lips. Costel couldn’t bear it. At ten at night he went down to the lorry on the pretext of checking the tyres and spent an hour listening to Spanish radio with his headphones on. Mrs Florica, who saw him from the window, called Ana to tell on him. Ana told her to leave him alone: some people calmed down that way.

Saturday 22 November dawned freezing. At half past eight, outside the Instituto Cervantes, about forty candidates were waiting on the pavement, with plastic folders, bottles of water and faces fit for a funeral. Costel was wearing the freshly ironed shirt he had worn for the Madrid fair. Señor Dan had two blue pens, two black ones, a pencil, a rubber, a wristwatch and a spare one in his pocket. Mrs Florica had made them sandwiches for the whole day. She had made twice as many as they could eat.

Señor Dan’s wife had come with them to the door. She was a small, energetic woman, a retired chemistry teacher who had marked exams for forty years and knew every trick. She checked their pens, straightened Costel’s collar and kissed her husband on the forehead, something that, according to Andrei, she hadn’t done in public since their wedding. Then she told them to go in calmly, because they were much better prepared than half her former pupils.

Before they went in, Ana gave each of them a sealed envelope. She told them not to open it until the break. Then she left, because she wasn’t allowed in the building during the exam. In the exam room, a young examiner with a Valladolid accent handed out the booklets and explained the rules at a speed Señor Dan found thoroughly unfair. Costel, on the other hand, understood every word. He knew it because, when the examiner made a joke about mobile phones, he was the only one who laughed.

The first paper was reading comprehension: seventy minutes, four texts, thirty-six questions. One of the texts was about old bookshops holding out in big cities. Señor Dan looked up from the paper and glanced at Costel, two rows ahead. Costel’s mouth was open. Both thought the same thing at the same time, but neither dared smile, because the examiner was watching them like a hawk. It was the part that went best for both of them.

Then came the listening comprehension, the part they feared most. The first recording was a lightning-fast conversation between two friends in a bar. The second, a radio programme about rural tourism. And the third, to Costel’s surprise, was the weather forecast from an Andalusian station: rain in the north, an easterly wind in the Strait, temperatures higher than normal for the time of year. Costel understood everything, word for word, better than he had ever understood it in the cab. He had to stop himself from clapping.

Señor Dan, on the other hand, didn’t do so well in the listening comprehension. In the second recording he lost his way in a sentence about country cottages and, trying to catch up, missed the answer to the next question. For a few seconds he felt his whole bridge collapsing. But he remembered the tips sheet: don’t try to understand everything. He took a deep breath, left that question blank and moved on to the next. In the end he calculated he had lost two points. For an engineer, two points were a tragedy; for the exam, hardly anything.

In the break they opened Ana’s envelopes. Inside each was a drawing by Rosa Elena. Costel’s showed an enormous lorry with a Spanish flag and the word “APROBADO” written in crooked letters. Señor Dan’s showed a bridge with two men on it, one with glasses and one with a cap, and underneath, the same word. Señor Dan folded the drawing very carefully and put it in his shirt pocket, next to the spare watch. He said nothing, but it showed on his face.

Written expression was the longest paper. They had to write two texts. For the second, they could choose between several topics, and one asked them to describe “a cultural event that moved you”. Costel didn’t hesitate: he wrote about the plaque on calle de las Huertas. He wrote short, correct sentences, as the tips sheet said. He used the pluperfect subjunctive twice and “de haberlo sabido” once. When he had finished, he counted the words with his finger. He had written twice as many as required. He had to cross out half.

Señor Dan, on the other hand, chose a topic about public transport in the cities of the future. He planned it like a bridge: first the pillars, that is, the arguments; then the deck, that is, the connectors; and finally the railing, that is, the conclusion. He had ten minutes to spare, which he used to check the accents one by one. Later he would confess to Ana that he had never checked anything so carefully, not even the plans of his first bridge.

The oral test was in the afternoon. Costel went in first. The examiner was an older man from Salamanca, with the calm voice of someone who has asked the same question ten thousand times. He showed him a photo and asked him to describe it. It was an old bookshop, with a wooden sign and a cat asleep in the window. Costel stared at it and burst out laughing. The examiner asked him what he found so funny. Costel replied that if he had ten minutes, he would tell him.

He had fifteen minutes, and he used them all. He talked about Andrés, about Ecaterina, about the hundred books in the lorry, about Zoltán crying in Hungary, about the fair, the funeral, the plaque. At first he went slowly, searching for words. Then, the more he talked, the faster they came. The examiner stopped taking notes after five minutes. At the end he took off his glasses and said he had been examining for thirty years and it was the first time a photo had told him such a long story. Then he cleared his throat and reminded him that he couldn’t tell him his mark.

Señor Dan got a photo of a crowded railway station. For the first two minutes almost nothing came out. He froze, repeated the same sentence twice and went bright red. The examiner patiently asked him how he had got to the exam that morning. Señor Dan said by metro, and that the Bucharest metro had a structural problem on line 1. And from then on there was no stopping him: he talked about tunnels, beams, bridges, Atocha station. He came out saying he didn’t know whether he had passed, but the examiner now knew a great deal about engineering.

At six in the evening they came out into the street. It was dark and bitterly cold, but the whole club was waiting on the pavement: Ana, Mihai, Rosa Elena with her camera, Mrs Florica with a flask of soup and Ecaterina, leaning on her stick, who had come even though the doctor had advised her not to go out in that cold. Rosa Elena took a photo of the two of them standing on the pavement, utterly exhausted, with the drawings peeping out of their pockets. It was the photo they would later hang in the lorry’s cab.

They had dinner at Ecaterina’s. Mrs Florica served the soup and made them tell her about the whole exam, question by question, although she didn’t understand a word of what they said. Costel told the weather forecast story three times, and each time the easterly wind in the Strait blew harder. Señor Dan told the metro story, and Mihai asked him whether there really was a structural problem on line 1. Señor Dan said no, he had made it up so he could talk about something he knew. Everyone stared at him. It was the first lie they had ever heard him tell.

At the end of dinner, Ecaterina brought out two parcels wrapped in brown paper, like the bookshop’s. Inside were two copies of Machado’s poems, in an old edition she had found in a second-hand bookshop in Bucharest. On the first page she had written the same thing in both: “For when you pass. And if you don’t pass, for then too.” Costel asked her why Machado. Ecaterina replied that he was the poet who best knew that the road is made by walking, and the two of them had made theirs in a lorry.

The results wouldn’t arrive for another two or three months. Ana explained that this was normal, that the Instituto Cervantes in Madrid marked all the exams in the world, and that the more candidates there were, the longer it took. Costel said he could wait. That he had waited forty years to study something properly, and two more months were nothing. Ecaterina, from her armchair, told him to be careful with that sentence, because she had once thought that too, and then it had been forty years.

Before going home, very late, Costel wrote a message to Andrei: “Exam done. Weather forecast, perfect. Now we wait.” Andrei replied from Madrid with a photo: the green sign in the hallway, with a note stuck to it that said “Good luck, Costel”. Underneath, another message, from Marta: “My grandfather would have said that whoever studies in a lorry passes anywhere.” Costel sat staring at his phone for a long time in the cab, with the engine off. Then, for the first time in three months, he switched off the radio and went to sleep.
